bibl.title: Sleep Differentially Affects Early and Late Neuronal Responses to Sounds in Auditory and Perirhinal Cortices

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: Auditory responses of neurons in auditory cortex and in the downstream perirhinal cortex, compared across wakefulness, NREM and REM sleep.
span.quote: For the above reasons, we set out to directly compare auditory responses in PRC neurons across wakefulness and natural sleep.

span.label: Auditory cortex responds to sound much the same asleep as awake - so where along the pathway does the sleeping brain actually stop listening?
span.quote: However, investigation of sensory responses downstream from sensory cortical regions at the level of neuronal spiking activity is still missing.

span.label: Perirhinal responses are attenuated by 47% in NREM and 36% in REM while auditory cortex barely changes - and response latency predicts the attenuation better than cortical region does.
span.quote: In addition, we find that the response latency of each neuronal cluster (typically <20 ms in AC and >40 ms in PRC) is correlated with the degree of NREM sleep attenuation, and better predicts attenuation than does cortical region.

span.label: existence
span.quote: We find that PRC exhibits robust attenuation of response magnitude in both NREM sleep and REM sleep, whereas AC neurons are only modestly affected by sleep.

span.label: sleep attenuation of auditory responses in high-order cortex
span.quote: The robust attenuation of late responses prevalent in PRC represents a novel neural correlate of sensory disconnection during sleep, opening new avenues for investigating the mediating mechanisms.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: Here we recorded spiking activity in 435 neuronal clusters evoked by acoustic stimuli in the perirhinal cortex (PRC) and in AC of freely behaving male rats across wakefulness and sleep.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NREM sleep imposes a graded, cumulative attenuation that builds up along the processing hierarchy rather than a single discrete gate at one anatomical station
span.quote: The robust correlation of NREM sleep attenuation with response latency suggests that NREM sleep may exert a gradual attenuation of cortical responses, rather than imposing a discrete “gate” at a specific brain region.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Breakdown of cortical effective connectivity in NREM sleep means signals lose more strength at each additional synapse, so responses arriving later are attenuated more
span.quote: The fact that late responses exhibit stronger attenuation in NREM sleep is in line with the notion of breakdown of cortical effective connectivity during NREM sleep ( Massimini et al., 2005 ) that may lead to greater attenuation with increasing synaptic connections.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the disconnection is not at the sensory front end: auditory cortex responds nearly as strongly asleep as awake, so whatever gates perception acts further downstream
span.quote: In addition, several recent studies in the auditory system showed that responses in the primary and secondary auditory cortex (AC) are comparable across wakefulness and natural sleep

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: perirhinal cortex is the candidate site because it is multimodal, downstream of several primary cortices, and carries intrinsic inhibition controlling flow to the hippocampus
span.quote: Moreover, it has been shown to contain intrinsic inhibitory mechanisms that affect information flow to the hippocampus ( de Curtis and Paré, 2004 ; Pelletier et al., 2004 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the operative variable is TIME not PLACE: whatever suppresses the response acts on late activity wherever it occurs, not on a particular region
span.quote: Beyond the separation according to cortical region, response latency in each neuronal cluster was correlated with the degree of NREM sleep attenuation, such that late (>40 ms) responses in all monitored regions diminished during NREM sleep.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the older explanation - thalamic gating - was already in trouble, because olfactory responses that bypass the thalamus are attenuated too
span.quote: However, this view was challenged by sleep attenuation of responses in the olfactory cortex that are not relayed through thalamus ( Murakami et al., 2005 ).

span.label: Stimulation was passive, so effects of behaviourally relevant or rewarded sounds were not assessed.
span.note: what this limits: any claim about behaviourally relevant sounds: WE USED A PASSIVE AUDITORY STIMULATION SCHEME WHERE SOUNDS WERE NOT ASSOCIATED WITH SPECIFIC BEHAVIORS OR REWARDS
span.quote: Of note, we used a passive auditory stimulation scheme where sounds were not associated with specific behaviors or rewards.

span.label: The latency-attenuation relationship found in NREM sleep did not hold in REM sleep.
span.note: what this limits: the latency-attenuation relationship outside NREM: IN REM SLEEP, ATTENUATION DID NOT CLEARLY FOLLOW RESPONSE LATENCY AS WAS THE CASE DURING NREM SLEEP (DATA NOT SHOWN)
span.quote: In REM sleep, attenuation did not clearly follow response latency as was the case during NREM sleep (data not shown), nor did we observe a significant difference between attenuation for neuronal pairs with different latencies recorded on same microelectrodes ( p = 0.07, 5% in early-responding neurons vs −20% in late-responding neurons).

span.label: The proposed REM-sleep explanation is offered as speculation.
span.note: what this limits: the REM explanation only: ALTHOUGH SPECULATIVE, IT IS POSSIBLE THAT, DURING REM SLEEP, ONGOING MNEMONIC ACTIVITY DURING DREAMING INTERFERES WITH BOTTOM-UP SENSORY PROCESSES
span.quote: For example, although speculative, it is possible that, during REM sleep, ongoing mnemonic activity during dreaming interferes with bottom-up sensory processes ( Nir and Tononi, 2010 ; Andrillon et al., 2016 ).

span.label: Ten rats, male only, in two strains.
span.note: what this limits: the population the result speaks for: EXPERIMENTS WERE PERFORMED IN 8 LONG-EVANS AND 2 WISTAR ADULT MALE RATS
span.quote: Experiments were performed in 8 Long–Evans and 2 Wistar adult male rats (250–350 g) individually housed in transparent Perspex cages with food and water available ad libitum .

span.label: The result is a correlate, and the paper says the mediating mechanism remains to be investigated.
span.note: what this limits: the causal reading: the finding REPRESENTS A NOVEL NEURAL CORRELATE OF SENSORY DISCONNECTION DURING SLEEP, with the mediating mechanism left to future work
span.quote: The robust attenuation of late responses prevalent in PRC represents a novel neural correlate of sensory disconnection during sleep, opening new avenues for investigating the mediating mechanisms.

span.label: Prior evidence about perirhinal auditory responses is inconsistent, with anaesthetised preparations failing to find them at all.
span.note: what this limits: any comparison with the anaesthetised perirhinal literature: SEPARATE STUDIES DURING ANESTHESIA DID NOT REVEAL SIGNIFICANT AUDITORY RESPONSES AS ONE MOVES VENTRALLY TOWARD RHINAL cortex, while waking studies find reliable responses
span.quote: While perirhinal neurons reliably respond to sounds during wakefulness ( Allen et al., 2007 ; Furtak et al., 2007 ), separate studies during anesthesia did not reveal significant auditory responses as one moves ventrally toward rhinal fissure ( Doron et al., 2002 ).

span.label: The literature the study enters is thin: few studies have examined sensory responses in natural sleep at the neuronal level at all.
span.note: what this limits: the evidence base this study joins: SURPRISINGLY, ONLY FEW STUDIES INVESTIGATED SENSORY RESPONSES DURING NATURAL SLEEP AT THE NEURONAL LEVEL
span.quote: Surprisingly, only few studies investigated sensory responses during natural sleep at the neuronal level ( Hennevin et al., 2007 ).

span.label: neurons with peak latencies in the 20-40 ms band DROPPED from the latency-based split, keeping only <20 ms and >40 ms
span.quote: leaving out neurons with peak latencies of 20–40 ms from the analysis based on latency to avoid ambiguity

span.label: the first second after each auditory stimulus EXCLUDED before smoothing when detecting OFF periods
span.quote: while excluding data immediately following (<1000 ms) auditory stimulation onset, to avoid false detections of auditory-induced reductions in firing as OFF periods

span.label: sleep
span.quote: Reduced behavioral responses to external sensory stimuli are an essential definition of sleep ( Carskadon and Dement, 2011 ) and are ubiquitous across the animal kingdom ( Cirelli and Tononi, 2008 ).

span.label: sensory disconnection
span.quote: The robust attenuation of late responses prevalent in PRC represents a novel neural correlate of sensory disconnection during sleep, opening new avenues for investigating the mediating mechanisms.

span.label: response latency
span.quote: In addition, we find that the response latency of each neuronal cluster (typically <20 ms in AC and >40 ms in PRC) is correlated with the degree of NREM sleep attenuation, and better predicts attenuation than does cortical region.

span.label: perirhinal cortex
span.quote: The PRC is a multimodal region downstream to several primary sensory cortices, where information converges from different sensory modalities to support higher brain functions, including perception and recognition memory ( Kealy and Commins, 2011 ).

span.label: auditory cortex
span.quote: In addition, several recent studies in the auditory system showed that responses in the primary and secondary auditory cortex (AC) are comparable across wakefulness and natural sleep

span.label: thalamic gating
span.quote: Early studies ( Gücer, 1979 ; Livingstone and Hubel, 1981 ) contributed to the “thalamic gating” model ( Steriade and McCarley, 1990 ), proposing that thalamic burst-mode activity and sleep spindle oscillations disrupt signal propagation to the cerebral cortex during sleep

span.label: targeted memory reactivation
span.quote: Targeted memory reactivation has been shown to influence hippocampal activity during sleep ( Rasch et al., 2007 ; Rothschild et al., 2017 ), suggesting that sounds can modulate activity in association cortices.

span.label: sleep - behavioural: the state in which an animal stops responding to what happens around it
span.quote: Reduced behavioral responses to external sensory stimuli are an essential definition of sleep ( Carskadon and Dement, 2011 ) and are ubiquitous across the animal kingdom ( Cirelli and Tononi, 2008 ).

span.label: sleep - neural: a set of vigilance states, NREM and REM, that attenuate responses by different amounts
span.quote: By contrast, PRC neuronal responses were robustly attenuated by 47% and 36% during NREM sleep and REM sleep, respectively.

span.label: disconnection - not an absence of processing: discriminative sensory processing continues while perception does not follow
span.quote: During sleep, external stimuli rarely affect perception ( Nir and Tononi, 2010 ), but it is also clear that some discriminative sensory processing persists ( Andrillon et al., 2016 ).

span.quote: The robust attenuation of late responses prevalent in PRC represents a novel neural correlate of sensory disconnection during sleep, opening new avenues for investigating the mediating mechanisms.

span.label: phenomenon: sensory disconnection during sleep, and where along the cortical hierarchy it takes effect
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. Recorded: sleep attenuation of auditory responses in high-order cortex — a second reading, verbatim-verified, disagreeing with the value on the record. Not applied - a person decides.
span.quote: Reduced behavioral responses to external sensory stimuli are an essential definition of sleep ( Carskadon and Dement, 2011 ) and are ubiquitous across the animal kingdom ( Cirelli and Tononi, 2008 ).

span.label: replicates → reports of preserved auditory cortical responses across vigilance states (Issa and Wang, 2008; Nir et al., 2015)
span.quote: In line with previous studies ( Issa and Wang, 2008 ; Nir et al., 2015 ), spiking responses in AC neurons exhibited similar profiles across vigilance states, whereas PRC neurons exhibited weaker responses in both NREM and REM sleep ( Fig. 4 ).

span.label: extends → Krom et al. (2018), the same early/late distinction observed in humans under light anesthesia
span.quote: In addition, a recent study comparing auditory responses at the neuronal level in humans across wakefulness and light anesthesia found a similar distinction between relatively preserved early responses in AC versus robust attenuation of late responses in association cortex ( Krom et al., 2018 ).

span.label: contradicts → Pereira et al. (2007), increased hippocampal responses to somatosensory microstimulation during sleep
span.quote: This discrepancy with the robust attenuation we find here in rat PRC may reflect differences in sensory modalities, or differences between natural stimuli used here versus ultra-short electrical stimulation.

span.label: contradicts → the "thalamic gating" model (Steriade and McCarley, 1990), which posits a discrete gate rather than graded attenuation
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS RESPONSE LATENCY. 'THE ROBUST CORRELATION OF NREM SLEEP ATTENUATION WITH RESPONSE LATENCY suggests that NREM sleep may exert A GRADUAL ATTENUATION of cortical responses, RATHER THAN IMPOSING A DISCRETE GATE at a specific brain region.' A gate predicts a step at one locus; the graded alternative predicts a monotone relationship with latency - so the two accounts differ on a measurable parameter rather than on a location. Q-448.
span.quote: The robust correlation of NREM sleep attenuation with response latency suggests that NREM sleep may exert a gradual attenuation of cortical responses, rather than imposing a discrete “gate” at a specific brain region.

span.label: replicates → prior findings that auditory cortex responses are comparable across wakefulness and sleep
span.quote: Neuronal responses in AC showed modest (∼10%) differences in response gain across vigilance states, replicating previous studies.

span.label: contradicts → the thalamic gating model of sleep-related sensory disconnection
span.quote: However, this view was challenged by sleep attenuation of responses in the olfactory cortex that are not relayed through thalamus ( Murakami et al., 2005 ).

span.label: extends → human imaging work showing attenuation downstream of sensory cortex during sleep
span.quote: However, investigation of sensory responses downstream from sensory cortical regions at the level of neuronal spiking activity is still missing.

span.quote: The robust attenuation of late responses prevalent in PRC represents a novel neural correlate of sensory disconnection during sleep, opening new avenues for investigating the mediating mechanisms.

span.label: RETRACTED (THE `to` ENDPOINT IS THE TAGGER'S PHRASE) · sleep —causes→ sensory disconnection
span.note: RETRACTED: THE `to` ENDPOINT IS THE TAGGER'S PHRASE. The edge is `sleep --causes--> sensory disconnection`. The span: 'By contrast, PRC NEURONAL RESPONSES WERE ROBUSTLY ATTENUATED BY 47% AND 36% DURING NREM SLEEP AND REM SLEEP, respectively.' `Sensory disconnection` does not occur - as a word or at all. What the sentence reports is a MEASURED ATTENUATION with two numbers attached; `sensory disconnection` is the interpretation those numbers are usually put to, supplied from knowledge of the literature. TRUE OF THE FIELD, UNSUPPORTED BY THE SPAN - and note the edge also drops the 47% and 36%, which are the only things the sentence actually establishes. Found by the neighbour query (Q-400). Q-423. — strength of the relation: 1
span.quote: By contrast, PRC neuronal responses were robustly attenuated by 47% and 36% during NREM sleep and REM sleep, respectively.

span.label: perirhinal cortex —contrasted-with→ auditory cortex
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS HOW FAR ALONG THE HIERARCHY THE SLEEP EFFECT BITES. 'RESPONSES IN AUDITORY CORTEX ONLY SHOWED MODEST CHANGES DURING SLEEP, WHEREAS SLEEP ROBUSTLY ATTENUATED THE RESPONSES OF NEURONS IN HIGH-LEVEL PERIRHINAL CORTEX.' The attenuation is graded along the pathway rather than switched on at one place, which is the same claim this record's [3] on claim_relations makes about latency - a gradual attenuation rather than a discrete gate. Q-486. · strength of the relation: 1 — RE-GROUNDS Sela2020-sleep-differentially-affects-early-and-late[0]: the relation was always stated, the endpoint names were not in the span.
span.quote: Responses in auditory cortex only showed modest changes during sleep, whereas sleep robustly attenuated the responses of neurons in high-level perirhinal cortex.

span.label: Mann-Whitney U test
span.quote: Unless stated otherwise, a two-tailed Mann–Whitney U test was used to assess statistical significance.

span.label: Mann-Whitney test (one-tailed)
span.quote: Then, a one-tailed Mann–Whitney test compared, for each millisecond within a 600 ms interval (500 ms of stimulus + 100 ms following it), the N values, against the entire N × 500 values in the 500 ms period preceding the stimulus.

span.label: false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons
span.term: false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: Multiple comparisons were corrected via false discovery rate ( Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001 ).

span.label: significance level (alpha)
span.quote: We corrected for the 600 multiple comparisons using false discovery rate ( Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001 ) with base α of 0.001.

span.label: Wilcoxon signed-rank test
span.quote: Analysis of baseline firing rates revealed that AC neurons exhibited 21%–26% higher firing rates during wakefulness (6.0 ± 0.6 Hz) or REM sleep (5.6 ± 0.6 Hz) compared with NREM sleep (4.4 ± 0.4 Hz, p values ≤ 10 −8 via signed-rank tests)

span.label: correlation

span.label: confidence interval

span.label: z score

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Quiet wake, NREM sleep, and REM sleep composed 15 ± 6.3%, 41 ± 6.2%, and 8 ± 2.4% of experiment time, respectively (mean ± SD; Fig. 2 B , C )

span.label: correlation

span.label: proportion

span.label: Auditory cortex responses changed only about 10% across vigilance states, whereas perirhinal cortex responses were cut by 47% in NREM sleep and 36% in REM sleep.
span.quote: Neuronal responses in AC showed modest (∼10%) differences in response gain across vigilance states, replicating previous studies. By contrast, PRC neuronal responses were robustly attenuated by 47% and 36% during NREM sleep and REM sleep, respectively.

span.label: Median gain factors quantified the perirhinal attenuation as -47% in NREM sleep and -36% in REM sleep, with confidence intervals excluding zero.
span.quote: PRC neurons showed attenuation with median gain factor of −47% (CI = [−56%, −34%]) in NREM sleep and −36% (CI = [−43%, −30%]) in REM sleep

span.label: Auditory cortex neurons showed only small median gain changes of -12% in NREM sleep and -6% in REM sleep.
span.quote: By contrast, AC neurons only exhibited modest changes, with median gain factor of −12% (CI = [−20%, −3%]), and −6% (CI = [−19%, 2%]) in NREM sleep and REM sleep, respectively.

span.label: Across all recorded neurons, the later a neuron's peak response latency, the more its response was attenuated in NREM sleep, a strong negative correlation.
span.quote: Next, we went beyond a binary separation to early- and late-responding neurons and found a significant correlation ( r = −0.55, p = 10 −15 ) between peak latency and NREM sleep gain attenuation

span.label: Neurons whose latency did not match their region behaved according to latency, not anatomy: late-responding auditory cortex neurons were attenuated by 43% while early-responding perirhinal neurons were attenuated by only 3%.
span.quote: We found that late-responding AC neurons show a substantial attenuation profile resembling that observed in PRC (gain factor of −43%, CI = [−60%, −25%]), whereas early-responding PRC neurons only showed modest attenuation in NREM sleep, as was observed in AC (gain factor of −3%, CI = [−16%, 33%]

span.label: Even for pairs of neurons recorded on the very same microwire, the late-responding member was attenuated roughly eightfold more in NREM sleep than the early-responding member, ruling out an electrode-position explanation.
span.quote: we found a robust (8-fold) difference in gain attenuation during NREM sleep such that early-responding neurons showed a modest average gain (−5.4 ± 9.8%) versus robust (−41 ± 8.6%) attenuation for late-responding neurons

span.label: Peak response latency was bimodal and tracked region: 85% of neurons peaking under 20 ms were in auditory cortex and 89% of those peaking over 40 ms were in perirhinal cortex.
span.quote: Responses of early-responding neurons with peak latencies <20 ms were mostly (85%) observed in AC, whereas the majority (89%) of late-responding neurons with peak latencies >40 ms were found in PRC

span.label: Baseline firing rates in auditory cortex were 21-26% higher in wakefulness and REM sleep than in NREM sleep.

span.label: Within NREM sleep, late-responding neurons responded more strongly to sounds delivered during local OFF periods than during ON periods.

span.quote: Here we recorded spiking activity in 435 neuronal clusters evoked by acoustic stimuli in the perirhinal cortex (PRC) and in AC of freely behaving male rats across wakefulness and sleep.

span.label: 47% (NREM) and 36% (REM) — attenuation of perirhinal auditory responses relative to wakefulness
span.quote: By contrast, PRC neuronal responses were robustly attenuated by 47% and 36% during NREM sleep and REM sleep, respectively.

span.label: ~10% — the much smaller change in auditory cortex response gain across vigilance states
span.quote: Neuronal responses in AC showed modest (∼10%) differences in response gain across vigilance states, replicating previous studies.

span.label: <20 ms in AC, >40 ms in PRC — typical response latencies, and the axis along which attenuation is organised
span.quote: In addition, we find that the response latency of each neuronal cluster (typically <20 ms in AC and >40 ms in PRC) is correlated with the degree of NREM sleep attenuation, and better predicts attenuation than does cortical region.

span.label: 10 rats — 8 Long-Evans and 2 Wistar adult males
span.quote: Experiments were performed in 8 Long–Evans and 2 Wistar adult male rats (250–350 g) individually housed in transparent Perspex cages with food and water available ad libitum .
